reading.body:
AI adoption in US churches is not tracked by any official census; it is measured by a patchwork of research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes.

The pattern is measurement by survey and platform rather than by census. Barna Group runs the closest thing to sector-wide survey data, Gloo reports deployment across thousands of US churches, and Hartford and Pew add congregational and public attitude data. Census BTOS includes religious and civic organisations in its service-sector series, but no better official measure exists yet.

This matters for AI because adoption in churches is real but diffuse, and every tradition is writing its own guidance. The data does not say how many congregations actually use AI, how much compute that use requires, or what it means for power demand. It also does not give a single adoption rate, because none exists.

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The only official adoption figure in this material comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which places religious organizations inside the broader Other services category, NAICS 81. In the latest period, 12.7% of firms in that category answered yes to whether they had used AI in the last two weeks, down from 15.0% in the prior period. That is the measured number, and it covers a wide range of other services firms alongside congregations, so it should be read as a ceiling rather than a precise count for churches. The Census Bureau notes that some values in this series are suppressed, and no finer breakdown for religious organizations alone appears in the data here.

What congregations actually do with AI is described mainly by the organizations that study and serve them. Barna Group, a Christian research organization, reports that nearly all pastors say a church should have guidelines for responsible AI use, while far fewer say their own church has them. Barna's research looks at how pastors are using AI and where guidelines may apply, which points to sermon preparation and administrative work as the practical territory. Gloo, which describes itself as delivering values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks for faith-based organizations and says it is used by thousands of US churches, frames AI as a foundational capability across its platform meant to support mission effectiveness and preserve relational ministry. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research, with a 45 year history of accurate research on churches and congregational life, is cited as regularly surveying congregational trends and digital adoption, though the excerpt itself offers no figures.

On money and vendors, the material is thin and should be treated as such. Gloo is the named commercial platform in this set, offering API-first support for inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows with dynamic model selection, and it is described here as the sector's tech platform. No funding totals, market sizes, or revenue figures appear anywhere in the JSON, so none can be reported. The concentration that is visible is organizational rather than financial: a small number of research bodies, Barna, Hartford, and Pew Research Center, plus the ethics network AI and Faith and the University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, produce most of what is known about the sector.

The ROI evidence the sources report is about labor and formation rather than dollars. A white paper from All Tech is Human and the Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics lab, Two Views of the Same Transformation, found that mid-level professionals described checking AI output as a growing and unrecognized share of their work, with some calling it babysitting AI slop, and that women reported carrying more of this glue work, which is missing from performance reviews. Executives in the same research described middle management as a layer to cut and then worried about distributed deskilling. Meghan Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher at Notre Dame, said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and about AI doing work faster and cheaper, and that some are trying to transcend work to devote time to family and hobbies. That is a caution about hidden costs, not a return calculation.

The risks and regulatory posture in this material are ethical and theological rather than legal. AI and Faith, a pluralist global network of faith leaders, scholars, technologists, ethicists, and educators, argues that the world's religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide AI development, and notes that for the 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation these issues are deeply spiritual as well as moral. It seeks to inject humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected both. Notre Dame's institute frames its work as promoting interdisciplinary research and policy leadership in AI and technology ethics and providing practical models for ethical design, development, and deployment. Pew Research Center's religion work in this set measures religious hostilities, restrictions on religion, and public attitudes, including that most US adults who attend services say they have recently heard clergy address a political or social issue, but it does not report AI regulation.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few modest conclusions. Adoption in the official data is real but limited, at 12.7% in the latest period for the broader Other services category, and it moved down from 15.0%, so this is not a sector in rapid measured takeup. The gap Barna identifies, that nearly all pastors want guidelines and far fewer have them, suggests governance is the first practical step rather than tool selection. The Notre Dame and All Tech is Human findings suggest budgeting for the human review work that AI output creates, because that work is currently invisible in performance reviews. Beyond that, the sources here do not report costs, savings, or deployment outcomes in congregations, and it is better to say less than to fill that space.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, brings together a multidisciplinary community to advance moral understanding and respond to pressing ethical issues, including work on artificial intelligence and technology ethics that engages stakeholders to develop practical models for ethical design and deployment. A white paper from All Tech is Human and the Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics lab, titled Two Views of the Same Transformation, reported that mid-level professionals described checking AI output as a growing and unrecognised part of their jobs, with some calling it "babysitting AI slop." That paper also found the glue work of a rollout is absent from performance reviews and that women reported carrying more of it, while executives described middle management as a layer to cut and then worried about distributed deskilling. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher at the University of Notre Dame who often meets AI leaders and developers, said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and about AI doing work faster and cheaper, and that some are trying to transcend work to spend their time on family and hobbies such as gardening and crafts.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group describes itself as a Christian research organisation producing data and insights on trends affecting faith, culture and ministry, alongside articles, reports, podcasts, courses and services. New Barna research examined how pastors use AI and where guidelines might apply. According to that research, nearly all pastors believe a church should have guidelines for responsible AI use, while far fewer report that their own church has them.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith describes itself as a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partner organisations working toward a future in which AI serves humankind under five strategic pillars. The organisation argues that these issues are deeply moral at root, and ,  for the 85 percent of the world's population it says claims a religious affiliation ,  deeply spiritual too, with the world's religions offering ancient wisdom to guide AI's development and use. It says it encourages, connects and equips tech creators, academic researchers, ethicists and theologians to engage with the moral and ethical questions around AI and related technologies, aiming to shape the discussion in thoughtful, life-affirming ways. A statement quoted on the page frames the goal as injecting "humility and historicity" into an industry that has often rejected both, and as a humanistic effort to bring faith-based, literary, classical and oral traditions to bear on what it calls possibly the most important technological transformation of our time.
